title: Commutative unipotent groups in characteristic zero are vector groups
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All groups are affine $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Assume $\operatorname{char}k=0$. Let $G$ be smooth, connected and commutative. Suppose there is a closed immersion of group schemes $G\hookrightarrow U_n$ for some $n\geq1$, where $U_n(R)$ is the group of upper triangular $n\times n$ matrices with diagonal entries $1$, for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$. Then for some integer $d\geq0$ there is an isomorphism of $k$-group schemes $\mathbf G_a^d\xrightarrow{\sim}G$. Here $\mathbf G_a(R)=(R,+)$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$ [def-sc-gm-ga], and $\mathbf G_a^0$ is the trivial group $1=\operatorname{Spec}k$.

source.place: Proposition 14.32 and Corollary 14.33, printed p.289. Only the commutative consequence is used; 14.32 is proved through the characteristic-zero central series of 14.21 and 14.24, independently of Corollary 14.55.

proof.text: For every smooth connected commutative group $V$ admitting a closed unitriangular embedding, put $\mathfrak v=T_eV$. By [lem-sfb-unipotent-exponential-construction] it is a finite-dimensional space of strictly upper triangular matrices and has a morphism $\exp_V:\mathfrak v_a\to V$. We prove that this morphism is an isomorphism by strong induction on $d=\dim_k\mathfrak v$, simultaneously for all such $V$ over the fixed field $k$. The trivial group has tangent space zero and its exponential is the identity between one-point schemes. For a nontrivial $V$, steps 2--6 below construct $N\simeq\mathbf G_a$ and a quotient satisfying the same hypotheses with tangent dimension $d-1$; in particular they show that a nontrivial $V$ cannot have $d=0$.

source.place: Proposition 14.32, printed p.289: induction, indexed here by tangent dimension; 14.31 constructs the morphism.

e1$. Then $H_{r+1}=1$, and the restricted coordinate homomorphism $p_{r+1}:H_r	o\mathbf G_a$ has trivial scheme-theoretic kernel. Factor it as $H_r\xrightarrow{u}I\hookrightarrow\mathbf G_a$ by [lem-sfb-affine-homomorphism-flat-image]. For every $k$-algebra $R$, if $u_R(x)=u_R(y)$ then $xy^{-1}$ lies in that trivial kernel, so $x=y$. Thus $u^*:k[I]	o k[H_r]$ is an epimorphism of commutative rings: maps out of $k[H_r]$ agreeing on $k[I]$ induce the same $k$-algebra structure on their target, and then agree by this injectivity on points. It is faithfully flat by the factorization. Apply [lem-sfb-faithfully-flat-ring-epimorphism-isomorphism] to conclude that $u$ is an isomorphism. In particular $I
e1$.

source.place: 14.21 proof, printed pp.284--285, using 6.49; make the last nontrivial intersection and its image explicit.

proof.text: If $I\subsetneq\mathbf G_a$, [lem-sfb-additive-subgroup-polynomial-quotient] gives a monic defining polynomial $P$ of positive degree $a$ with $P(X+Y)=P(X)+P(Y)$ and $P(0)=0$. If $a>1$, the coefficient of $X^{a-1}Y$ on the left is $a\ne0$ and on the right is zero, a contradiction in characteristic zero. Thus $a=1$ and $P(T)=T$, which gives $I=1$, also a contradiction. Hence $I=\mathbf G_a$. Set $N=H_r$ and let $a:\mathbf G_a\simeq N$ be the resulting isomorphism. It is a closed subgroup of $V$, and is central since $V$ is commutative. The standard embedding $t\mapsto I+tE_{12}$ of $\mathbf G_a$ has square-zero tangent matrices, so the finite exponential formula in [lem-sfb-unipotent-exponential-construction] gives $\exp_{\mathbf G_a}(t)=t$. Its naturality for $a$ therefore identifies $\exp_N:(T_eN)_a\to N$ with $a$, using $\mathrm da:k\simeq T_eN$. In particular $\dim_k T_eN=1$.

source.place: Remark 14.24(a), printed p.285; Proposition 14.32, printed p.289, base case Ga. The coefficient proof also covers nonreduced subgroup schemes.

proof.text: The identity point of $V$ and [lem-sbc-connected-rational-point-geometrically-connected] make $V$ geometrically connected. Since $N$ is central, [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] gives $q:V\to Q=V/N$, an affine finite-type, smooth geometrically connected group, with kernel $N$ and with $q$ faithfully flat and finitely presented. It also gives the torsor isomorphism $(v,n)\mapsto(v,vn):V\times N\simeq V\times_QV$. Commutativity descends to $Q$: any two sections lift fppf locally along $q$, where their commutator is the identity; equality then descends. The torsor is locally trivial on the fppf cover $V\to Q$, with its diagonal section. Over $Q$, $N_Q\simeq\mathbf G_{a,Q}$ is smooth affine and finitely presented: a polynomial coordinate lifts across every square-zero quotient. Therefore [lem-sfb-smooth-affine-group-torsor-representability] applied over $Q$ shows that $q$ itself is smooth. Smoothness of $\mathbf G_a$ also follows directly from [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]: its one polynomial coordinate can be lifted across any square-zero quotient.

source.place: Proposition 14.32, printed p.289, quotient and torsor square; smoothness of a torsor under a smooth group supplies the tangent lifting argument.

proof.text: To verify unipotence of $Q$ over $k$, first note that smoothness of $V$ is preserved by field extension directly from [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]: forget the extension-field structure in a lifting square, lift over $k$, and pair that lift with the prescribed map to the new base; tensoring a finite presentation preserves its generators and relations. Extend the quotient to an algebraic closure $\bar k$ using [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]. Apply [lem-sfb-unipotent-normal-quotient-image] with its $A=N=V_{\bar k}$, $D=I=Q_{\bar k}$, $f=u=q_{\bar k}$ and $j=\mathrm{id}$. Its hypotheses hold: $V_{\bar k}$ is smooth, connected and unitriangular, and $q_{\bar k}$ is faithfully flat. It yields unipotence of $Q_{\bar k}$. The field-extension detection and faithful-matrix criterion of [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial] give unipotence of the smooth group $Q$. Apply [lem-sfb-normal-subgroup-representation-kernel] to the trivial subgroup of $Q$, obtaining $\rho:Q\to\mathrm{GL}_{r,k}$ with trivial kernel, hence injective on every algebra's points. Its geometric matrices are unipotent: the definition of unipotence just verified gives a closed immersion $i':Q_{\bar k}\hookrightarrow\mathcal U_{n',\bar k}$, injective on all $\bar k$-algebra points with $(i'(g)-I)^{n'}=0$ for $g\in Q(\bar k)$, and [lem-sfb-rational-representation-unipotent-point] with $K=\bar k$, faithful $i'$ and $r=\rho_{\bar k}$ makes every $\rho(g)$, $g\in Q(\bar k)$, unipotent. Thus [lem-sfb-geometric-unipotence-unitriangular-embedding] gives a closed unitriangular embedding of $Q$ over $k$. This verifies precisely the embedding hypothesis required by the induction, rather than just an embedding after field extension.

source.place: 14.7 and 14.9, printed p.282: quotients and field extensions of unipotent groups; used implicitly for G/Ga in 14.32.

proof.text: The tangent sequence is $0\to\mathfrak n\xrightarrow{\mathrm di}\mathfrak v\xrightarrow{\mathrm dq}\mathfrak q\to0$, where $\mathfrak n=T_eN$ and $\mathfrak q=T_eQ$ [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space]. Indeed a dual-number point of $V$ mapping to the identity in $Q$ factors uniquely through the scheme-theoretic fibre $N$, which proves injectivity and the kernel assertion. For surjectivity, a vector of $\mathfrak q$ gives a map $\operatorname{Spec}k[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2\to Q$ whose closed point is the identity. Smoothness of $q$ and the lifting property in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], applied to the identity $\operatorname{Spec}k\to V$, lift it to a vector of $\mathfrak v$. The maps are linear by the tangent-space definition. Step 3 now gives $\dim\mathfrak q=d-1$; thus nontrivial $V$ forces $d\geq1$, completing the zero-dimensional base case. Choose a linear section $s:\mathfrak q\to\mathfrak v$ of $\mathrm dq$ by lifting a basis. Then every element of $R\otimes\mathfrak v$ is uniquely $s(y)+\mathrm di(z)$ with $y\in R\otimes\mathfrak q$ and $z\in R\otimes\mathfrak n$, since this direct-sum decomposition tensors to every $k$-algebra $R$.

source.place: 10.14, printed p.190, tangent kernel sequence; the right-surjectivity needed in 14.32 is expanded directly by smooth infinitesimal lifting (Stacks Tag 02H0, definition-formally-smooth).

proof.text:
By induction $\exp_Q:\mathfrak q_a\to Q$ is an isomorphism, since step 5 verifies all group hypotheses and step 6 strictly lowers the induction integer. Naturality in [lem-sfb-unipotent-exponential-construction] gives
$$q\circ\exp_V=\exp_Q\circ\mathrm dq,\qquad i\circ\exp_N=\exp_V\circ\mathrm di.$$
In the commutative group $V$, any two tangent matrices commute. To check this without assuming a Lie-bracket theorem, use $B=R[\epsilon,\eta]/(\epsilon^2,\eta^2)$. The points $I+\epsilon X$ and $I+\eta Y$ belong to $V(B)$ by the tangent-coordinate description in that node. Their commutator is $I+\epsilon\eta(XY-YX)$. Commutativity of $V(B)$ and the freeness of $B$ on $1,\epsilon,\eta,\epsilon\eta$ force $XY-YX=0$. The commuting-vector identity of the same node therefore gives $\exp_V(X+Y)=\exp_V(X)\exp_V(Y)$ for every $R$. In particular $\exp_V(s(y)+\mathrm di(z))=\exp_V(s(y))i(\exp_N(z))$.

source.place: 14.31, formula (93) and the naturality square; 14.32, printed p.289, equivariance and commutative clause. Mixed-dual-number calculation writes out why the tangent matrices commute.

proof.text: Here is an explicit inverse, so no torsor-comparison theorem is left implicit. For $v\in V(R)$ put $y=\exp_Q^{-1}(q(v))$ and $t=\exp_V(s(y))$. The naturality square gives $q(t)=q(v)$, so $t^{-1}v\in N(R)$ by the kernel clause of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]. Put $z=\exp_N^{-1}(t^{-1}v)$ and $F(v)=s(y)+\mathrm di(z)$. These formulas are morphisms of schemes: the factorization of $t^{-1}v$ through the closed kernel is given by its defining fibre square, and all the other operations are morphisms already constructed. Step 7 gives $\exp_V(F(v))=t(t^{-1}v)=v$. Conversely, for $X=s(y)+\mathrm di(z)$, that same formula gives $q(\exp_V(X))=\exp_Q(y)$ and $t^{-1}\exp_V(X)=\exp_N(z)$, so $F(\exp_V(X))=X$. Thus $\exp_V$ is an isomorphism of schemes. Step 7 proves it respects multiplication, so it is an isomorphism of group schemes. This completes the induction.

source.place: Proposition 14.32, printed p.289: expand the equivariant torsor-isomorphism argument (the source cites 2.71) using a linear section and the already proved exponential on the quotient.

proof.text: Apply the induction result to the given $G$. Choose a $k$-basis $b_1,\ldots,b_d$ of $T_eG$. The coordinate map $(r_1,\ldots,r_d)\mapsto\sum r_jb_j$ and its inverse coordinate functionals identify its additive vector scheme with $\mathbf G_a^d$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Composing this isomorphism with $\exp_G$ gives the required $\mathbf G_a^d\simeq G$. When $d=0$, both the vector scheme and $G$ are the trivial group by the induction's zero case; hence the empty-product clause is included.
